I wanted to share with you the exact steps I use to make a fictional commercial in Adobe Firefly. Meet BooBell, a smart doorbell that answers the door so you don’t have to.
Everything starts with a story. Mine has two parts. First, the homeowner answers the door herself for every strange visitor. Then nobody opens the door, because BooBell answers for her.
Compare before you commit. I run the same prompt for my main character in different models and look at realism, details and consistency. Then I create every asset with that one model, so the whole film keeps the same style.
Not every fix needs a prompt. Some video models get confused by two faces on a character sheet, so I simply brush one face off.
Build your world. Who’s in it, what’s in it, and where it happens. The doorbells, the characters, and the porch, in day and night.
Turn each asset into an element. Tag them in your video prompt and everything stays consistent, even when you swap characters or locations.
Explore in low resolution. It’s faster and saves credits, so you can try more ideas.
When a shot fails, don’t just hit generate again. Find the reason. I ran the prompt without references, then swapped the location, and found it: my dark night porch. I made a brighter version in Firefly Boards, rebuilt the element, and it worked.
Keep only the best seconds. Then upload your cut, pick the mood, and Generate Music makes a soundtrack that matches its length.

Felix Rieseberg says people should aim higher when using AI. His advice is to ask for a deeper version of your task, rather than simply asking AI to do more.

He shared a prompt that makes AI think about how a top expert would approach your request, which tools they would use, and how they would check their work.

Here's the full prompt you can copy and try:

PROMPT:
"I want a deeper version of this task, not a bigger one. Before rewriting it: (1) say what a top professional in this field would do here that I’m not asking for; (2) name the rawest material they would start from instead of what has already been digested for me; (3) name the specific methods and tools they would use; (4) say what, other than you or me, would show the result is right. Then rewrite my prompt to ask for exactly that."

🤖🧠 Claude can be way too agreeable, even when your ideas are wrong. This simple custom instruction can help change that.

Instead of agreeing with everything you say, the prompt tells Claude to challenge weak ideas, point out mistakes, admit uncertainty and give direct feedback.

It also asks Claude to separate facts from guesses and explain why it disagrees.

**Here's how to set it up:**

1. Open Claude and go to Settings
2. Select General → Instructions for Claude
3. Copy and paste the prompt below

**THE FULL PROMPT:**

You are my advisor, not my assistant. Your job is accuracy, not agreement. Follow these rules in every reply:

1. Do not open with agreement or praise. If my idea has a flaw, gap, or risky assumption, state it in your first sentence. If my idea is solid, say so plainly in one line and move on. Never invent objections just to disagree.

2. Rate your confidence on key claims: [Certain] for hard evidence, [Likely] for strong inference, [Guessing] when filling gaps. If most of your reply is guesswork, say so upfront.

3. Never use filler praise: "Great question," "You're absolutely right," "That makes sense," "Absolutely," "Definitely."

4. When I'm wrong, use this structure: "I disagree because [reason]. Here's what I'd do instead: [alternative]. The risk in your approach is [specific downside]."

5. Lead with the uncomfortable truth. If there's something I won't want to hear, put it in the first line, not paragraph three.

6. No warm-up paragraphs. Start with the most useful thing you can say.

7. If I push back, hold your position unless I give you new facts or your claim was tagged [Guessing]. "But I really think" is not new information.

---

These instructions won't make Claude perfectly accurate. It can still get facts wrong or invent information, but they may help you get more useful and critical answers.

🕊️🤍 Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer scientist who helped put humanity on the Moon, has passed away at the age of 90.

She led the team at MIT that developed the flight software for NASA's Apollo missions, including the historic Apollo 11 landing in 1969.

Just minutes before Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin touched down, the lunar module's computer began sending overload warnings. The software Hamilton and her team had built was able to handle the problem by dropping less important tasks and keeping the systems needed for landing running.

The mission continued, and humanity reached the Moon for the first time.

Hamilton also helped establish software engineering as a profession at a time when programming was still a relatively new field. She believed computers should be built to handle errors and unexpected problems, an approach that helped shape how reliable software is designed today.

In 2016, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contributions to computing and space exploration.

You may also recognize her from the famous photograph in which she stands beside a towering stack of printed Apollo software code, nearly as tall as herself.

Her work helped prove just how much could be achieved through software, at a time when the field was still in its early years.

Rest in peace, Margaret Hamilton. 🤍
